name: assembly-over-eskibeat
idea: Keep exactly what Kai liked: a whole primary-school assembly of around 200 children, aged 7 to 11, singing the hymn in flat, bored, London-accented unison, dutiful and blasé in the way of Another Brick in the Wall's school choir, recorded in an echoey school hall. Swap the piano out entirely for an early-2000s eskibeat grime instrumental at 140 BPM: a raw square-wave bass in short stabs, dry eski clicks on the off-beats, a sparse clap on 2 and 4, and one icy repeating synth stab, with lots of empty space. The children stay in strict hymn time, unaware of the beat, so the mismatch is the joke. The beat cuts dead after the last line ('sleep in a bin'), so nothing rings on. Exclude piano, organ, adult vocals, rap and pads.

name: playground-clapping-drill
idea: Not a choir: five or six ten-year-olds in a playground doing the hymn as a hand-clapping skipping rhyme, sing-song and half-chanted, giggly but deadpan, with real hand claps and a skipping rope slapping the tarmac as the only acoustic sounds. Under them is a dark UK drill beat (half-time feel, snare on 3, sliding 808 bass glides, skittering hats, an ominous minor two-note bell or string riff) that feels like it belongs to a much harder song. The kids' bounce and the beat's menace sit in two different worlds. Short and tight, the four lines and out, about 15 seconds. Exclude piano, organ, adult voices and choir reverb.

name: chopped-choir-sample-riddim
idea: The children aren't performing live: they're a sample. It sounds like a grime producer in a bedroom in 2004 found a scratchy old school-assembly record of a children's choir, then pitched it up slightly and chopped it over a cold riddim. The voice is a distant, lo-fi, vinyl-crackled mixed children's choir in an old-fashioned prim English register, line endings clipped by the chop. The music is a minimal grime riddim at 140 with square-wave sub stabs, a stuttering string-preset stab, gunshot-style rewind percussion and a moment where everything drops out but the sample. The whole thing should feel like dystopian found footage: innocent voices owned and repurposed by the machine. Exclude piano, live organ, adult vocals and rap.

name: one-bored-kid-in-the-dark
idea: One kid alone: a single eight-year-old boy with a broad London accent, singing the hymn completely unbothered, a bit flat and lazy, almost bored, as if made to do it at the front of class, very close and dry on the mic. The music is the grimiest, most dystopian version possible: nearly empty, a slow detuned square-wave bass drone that only moves on the downbeats, a single distorted kick, one cold metallic synth ping, distant sirens and tower-block reverb, closer to dark sublow than a busy beat. The scale is the point: one tiny careless voice against a huge bleak space. It ends with the bass cutting out under 'bin' and nothing after. Exclude piano, choir, harmonies, adult voices, pads and rap.
